the simultaneous decisions to provide informal care for elderly parents and to provide non-financial child support, as well as with women's participation decisions.

the Mexican labor force participation rate will increase, but the caregiving rate will remain stable.
the Mexican elderly population is not yet a significant burden to the family and society in terms of caregiving and support.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, as in the case of the United States, Mexican women are likely to continue to be the main providers of informal support for the elderly and children.
the decision to work or not is not only determined by the economic conditions of the household but it also depends on the care needs of family members.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, as the number of older people increases in the future, the number of caregivers is likely to decrease, which could have negative consequences for informal care provision in Mexico.
the decision to provide informal elderly and childcare support is a complex decision that is not easily captured by a simple model.
